course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: The Global Tapestry
unit.description: Explore how societies organized power, shared beliefs, and built their economies across the world.

firstTopic.summary: Song China: an enduring government, changing economy, and influential culture.

topic.title: Africa
topic.summary: African kingdoms and cities, connected by agriculture, commerce, and varied beliefs.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Which comparison of Mali and the Hausa city-states is accurate?
choices: Both had one shared ruler throughout 1200-1450.
Mali developed an empire, while Hausa cities retained separate rulers.
Neither society participated in regional exchange.
Every Hausa city was governed by an Inca official.
questions.explanation: These societies organized authority at different scales. Economic and cultural links did not require political unity.

questions.prompt: How did trans-Saharan exchange contribute to Mali’s political power?
choices: Revenue from commerce helped sustain rulers, armies, and administration.
Gold automatically eliminated disputes over succession.
Caravans replaced the need for agricultural producers.
Trade prevented religious and cultural connections.
questions.explanation: Rulers could use commercial revenue as one source of resources. Agriculture and political organization remained necessary.

questions.prompt: How could Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage support his authority?
choices: It made all Malian subjects immediately Muslim.
It transferred the Malian throne to the pope.
It ended all local traditions associated with kingship.
It strengthened his visible Islamic identity and connections with influential religious networks.
questions.explanation: The pilgrimage connected sacred prestige with international relationships. It did not produce complete religious uniformity.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of Swahili cities best accounts for African and imported cultural elements?
choices: Foreign goods prove that Africans could not build urban centers.
Arabic vocabulary means Swahili is not a Bantu language.
Local communities actively shaped cities connected to overseas exchange.
Islamic influence meant all coastal cities had one government.
questions.explanation: Connections can influence language and institutions without removing local agency or separate governments.

questions.prompt: What would imported ceramics found at Great Zimbabwe most directly suggest?
choices: The site was located on the Mediterranean coast.
Connections between an inland center and distant exchange networks.
The buildings were necessarily constructed by foreign rulers.
Its population relied exclusively on imported food.
questions.explanation: Imported objects support exchange connections, often through intermediaries. They do not establish who built or ruled the site.

questions.prompt: How do Lalibela’s churches challenge the claim that African state building relied exclusively on Islam?
choices: They demonstrate Christian patronage linked with Ethiopian kingship.
They prove religion never influenced any African state.
They show that all African rulers followed the Roman pope.
They date exclusively to European colonial rule.
questions.explanation: Ethiopia provides a specific Christian example within Africa’s broader religious diversity.

questions.prompt: Why should a historian examine the context of a griot’s account?
choices: Oral sources contain no usable historical information.
Written sources are always free of perspective.
Every performance was a transcript made by a court scribe.
Its audience and transmission can shape how rulers and events are remembered.
questions.explanation: Oral histories can preserve important evidence, but their context matters. The same principle applies to written and material sources.

questions.prompt: What is a problem with saying kin-based societies had no government?
choices: It assumes they always had an elected national parliament.
It understates their universal use of Chinese examinations.
It overlooks institutions that organized decisions and resolved disputes.
It overlooks their permanent political unity with Ethiopia.
questions.explanation: Political institutions can operate through elders, chiefs, and lineages without a single centralized empire.

Inland southern Africa.
The northern European coast.
The island of Java.
questions.explanation: Its inland location makes connections through coastal intermediaries important.

questions.prompt: Which tradition was important to medieval Ethiopian kingship?
choices: Christianity.
Neo-Confucian examination learning.
Maya calendrical kingship.
The Bhakti movement as a state religion.
questions.explanation: Christian institutions and claims to sacred ancestry supported rulers.

questions.prompt: What connected many Swahili cities to distant markets?
choices: The Grand Canal of China.
Inca roads across the Andes.
The English manorial court.
Indian Ocean exchange.
questions.explanation: Coastal cities linked African producers with overseas merchants.
